Neural Inverse Operators for Solving PDE Inverse Problems

 

Roberto Molinaro 1  Yunan Yang 2  Björn Engquist 3  Siddhartha Mishra 1 4 

††footnotetext: 1Seminar for Applied Mathematics (SAM), ETH, Zürich. 2Institute for Theoretical Studies (ITS), ETH Zürich. 3Department of Mathematics and the Oden Institute, The University of Texas at Austin, USA. 4ETH AI Center, ETH, Zürich. Correspondence to: Roberto Molinaro <roberto.molinaro@sam.math.ethz.ch>.
Abstract

A large class of inverse problems for PDEs are only well-defined as mappings from operators to functions. Existing operator learning frameworks map functions to functions and need to be modified to learn inverse maps from data. We propose a novel architecture termed Neural Inverse Operators (NIOs) to solve these PDE inverse problems. Motivated by the underlying mathematical structure, NIO is based on a suitable composition of DeepONets and FNOs to approximate mappings from operators to functions. A variety of experiments are presented to demonstrate that NIOs significantly outperform baselines and solve PDE inverse problems robustly, accurately and are several orders of magnitude faster than existing direct and PDE-constrained optimization methods.

1 Introduction.

Partial differential equations (PDEs) are ubiquitous as mathematical models in the sciences and engineering Evans (2010). Often, solving PDEs entails solving the so-called forward problem. That is, given inputs such as initial and boundary conditions, coefficients, and sources, compute (observables of) the solution of the PDE. However, in many important contexts in applications, one is instead interested in solving the so-called inverse problem Isakov (2017). That is, given measurements of (observables of) the solution of a PDE, infer the underlying inputs.

A large class of such inverse problems takes the following abstract form: given observables as operators (mappings between function spaces), infer the underlying input coefficient (functions) of the associated PDE. A prototypical example is the well-studied Calderón Problem Uhlmann (2009) that arises in electrical impedance tomography (EIT) in medical imaging. Here, the observable is the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) operator that maps the voltage on the boundary to the current, and one is interested in inferring the underlying conductivity field. A related example is inverse wave scattering for geophysical applications. Other examples include optical tomography Lai et al. (2019) where the observable is the so-called Albedo operator, and one needs to infer the scattering and absorption coefficients of the underlying medium. Another prominent example arises in seismic imaging in geophysics Yilmaz (2011) where the observable is the source-to-receiver (StR) operator, and the task at hand is to infer the underlying sub-surface properties such as wave velocity or material density. In many of these examples, the solution to the resulting inverse problem is unique and stable if and only if the inverse problem is posed as a mapping from operators to functions.

Given the nonlinear nature of most of these inverse problems, analytical solution formulas are not available except in some simple cases. Instead, iterative numerical algorithms based on the PDE-constrained optimization are commonly used to approximate the solution Chavent (2010). These algorithms repeatedly apply the forward and adjoint PDE solvers to converge to the unknown coefficient. However, a large number of iterations might be necessary, which leads to prohibitively high computational costs as numerous calls to PDE solvers are very expensive, particularly in two and three space dimensions. Moreover, these iterative algorithms can be sensitive to the choice of initial coefficient. Given these factors, the design of alternative approaches to solving inverse problems is imperative.

Data-driven approximation of PDEs is rapidly emerging as a powerful paradigm. Most of the available results pertain to forward problems for PDEs. A particularly popular framework is operator learning, where one seeks to learn the underlying forward solution operator of the PDE from data. Existing approaches to operator learning include Deep operator networks (DeepONet) Lu et al. (2021); Mao et al. (2020); Cai et al. (2021) and their variants, as well as the so-called neural operators Kovachki et al. (2021b), which include the widely used Fourier Neural Operators (FNO) and its variants Li et al. (2021b); Pathak et al. (2022). Graph neural network-based algorithms Boussif et al. (2022); Brandstetter et al. (2022) are also emerging as an alternative.

Given the widespread success of operator learning and other deep learning-based algorithms in the context of forward problems for PDEs, it is natural to investigate their utility in learning the solutions of the corresponding inverse problems from data. However, this task is very challenging as existing operator learning algorithms map functions to functions. On the other hand, the aforementioned inverse problems are only well-defined as maps from operators to functions. Hence, one needs non-trivial modifications of existing operator learning architectures to handle inverse problems. This is precisely the rationale for the current paper, where our main contributions are the following.

  • •

    Motivated by the underlying mathematical structure of the considered class of inverse problems, we propose a novel architecture, termed as Neural Inverse Operators (NIOs), for learning solutions of these inverse problems from data. NIOs compose (stack) two existing architectures, DeepONet and FNO, in order to map operators to functions.

  • •

    We test NIOs extensively on a suite of problems, including the Calderón problem in EIT, inverse wave scattering for object detection, reconstructing the absorption and scattering coefficients in optical tomography, and seismic wave migration to infer sub-surface properties. We show that NIO significantly outperforms baselines on all these benchmarks.

  • •

    Given the inherent sensitivity of PDE inverse problems to noise and perturbations, we also demonstrate empirically that NIO is robust with respect to these factors as well as to the number and location of sensors and underlying grid resolutions. Moreover, we also show that, unlike baselines, NIO can handle fluctuations in the number of input measurements as well as generalize out-of-distribution without any significant loss of accuracy. Furthermore, NIO is found to be several orders of magnitude faster while still being more accurate than traditional PDE-constrained optimization methods.

Thus, we propose a new learning framework for the fast, robust and accurate solution of PDE inverse problems.

2 A Class of Inverse Problems.

2.1 Mathematical Framework.

Let D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a bounded open set, with (smooth) boundary ∂D\partial D. Let T>0T>0 and Ω=D\Omega=D or Ω=D×(0,T)\Omega=D\times(0,T), depending on whether the PDE is time-(in)dependent. Correspondingly, ∂Ω=∂D\partial\Omega=\partial D or ∂Ω=∂D×(0,T)\partial\Omega=\partial D\times(0,T), respectively. Let a∈𝒜⁡(D)a\in\mathcal{A}(D), with 𝒜\mathcal{A} denoting a suitable function space over DD, be a coefficient. Then, an abstract PDE can be written as

𝒟a​(u)=s,ℬ⁡(u)=g,\mathcal{D}_{a}(u)=s,\quad\mathcal{B}(u)=g, (1)

where u∈𝒰⁡(Ω)u\in\mathcal{U}(\Omega) is the solution, s∈𝒮⁡(Ω)s\in\mathcal{S}(\Omega) is the source term and g∈𝒢⁡(∂Ω)g\in\mathcal{G}(\partial\Omega) is the boundary condition, for the PDE (1). Here, 𝒟a:𝒰↦ℱ\mathcal{D}_{a}:\mathcal{U}\mapsto\mathcal{F} and ℬ:𝒰↦𝒢\mathcal{B}:\mathcal{U}\mapsto\mathcal{G} are the differential and boundary operators, respectively and 𝒰,𝒮,𝒢\mathcal{U},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{G} are suitable function spaces, defined over their respective domains.

The forward problem for the abstract PDE (1) amounts to the following: given the coefficient a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, source term s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and boundary condition g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, find the solution u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} of the PDE (1). Often, one is interested in not only the solution itself but also observables of the solution, which can be measured in practice. Since measurements are usually easier to perform at boundaries, a particularly relevant class of such observables are given by the following boundary observation operator,

Λa:𝒢⁡(∂Ω)↦ℋ⁡(∂Ω),\Lambda_{a}:\mathcal{G}(\partial\Omega)\mapsto\mathcal{H}(\partial\Omega), (2)

which maps the boundary data g∈𝒢⁡(∂Ω)g\in\mathcal{G}(\partial\Omega) to a measurement Λa​(g)=h⁡(u)∈ℋ⁡(∂Ω)\Lambda_{a}(g)=h(u)\in\mathcal{H}(\partial\Omega), a function space on ∂Ω\partial\Omega. Thus, for a fixed coefficient aa (and source ss), solving the forward problem amounts to solving the PDE (1), with a given boundary data gg to obtain the solution uu and then post-processing uu to compute the boundary observation operator h​(u)=Λa​(g)h(u)=\Lambda_{a}(g). Hence, one can rewrite the forward problem associated with the PDE (1) to obtain the map,

ℱ:𝒜⁡(D)↦ℒ⁡(𝒢⁡(∂Ω),ℋ⁡(∂Ω)),a↦ℱ⁡(a)=Λa,\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{A}(D)\mapsto\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{G}(\partial\Omega),\mathcal{H}(\partial\Omega)\right),~a\mapsto\mathcal{F}(a)=\Lambda_{a}, (3)

where Λa\Lambda_{a} is the boundary observation operator (2) and ℒ⁡(X,Y)\mathcal{L}(X,Y) denotes continuous operators between function spaces XX and YY.

In practice, one is often interested in the inverse problem associated with the PDE (1). For instance, in tomography (imaging), one needs to infer the unknown coefficient aa from some measurements of the solution uu. In general, this problem is ill-posed, and a single instance (or small number) of boundary conditions gg and measurements h⁡(u)h(u) of the corresponding solutions uu, do not suffice in inferring the underlying coefficient aa. Instead, many deep mathematical results have provided suitable frameworks where such inverse problems can be well-posed. The inverse map for the forward problem (3) takes the form

ℱ−1:ℒ⁡(𝒢⁡(∂Ω),ℋ⁡(∂Ω))↦𝒜⁡(D),Λa↦a=ℱ−1​(Λa),\mathcal{F}^{-1}:\mathcal{L}\left(\mathcal{G}(\partial\Omega),\mathcal{H}(\partial\Omega)\right)\mapsto\mathcal{A}(D),~\Lambda_{a}\mapsto a=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a}), (4)

The rigorous guarantee of the existence and, more importantly, the uniqueness of this inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1}, for a large class of PDEs, is a crowning achievement of the mathematical theory of inverse problems Isakov (2017). Moreover, one can also show Lipschitz or Hölder-stability of the inverse problem by proving estimates of the form,

‖ℱ−1​(a)−ℱ−1​(a¯)‖ℒ∼‖a−a¯‖𝒜α,0<α≤1.\|\mathcal{F}^{-1}(a)-\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\overline{a})\|_{\mathcal{L}}\sim\|a-\overline{a}\|_{\mathcal{A}}^{\alpha},0<\alpha\leq 1. (5)

In some cases, the right-hand side of the above stability estimate is replaced by a logarithm of ‖a−a¯‖𝒜\|a-\overline{a}\|_{\mathcal{A}}, which only guarantees (weak) logarithmic stability.

After presenting this abstract framework, we provide four concrete examples of PDE inverse problems (see SM Figures 4-14 for illustrations) to which this abstract framework applies.

2.2 Calderón Problem (EIT).

Let the coefficient 0<a∈C2​(D)0<a\in C^{2}(D) represent the conductivity of the underlying medium (domain D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}) and the associated PDE (1) is the following elliptic equation,

−∇⋅(a(z)∇u)=0,\displaystyle-\nabla\cdot\Big(a(z)\nabla u\Big)=0, z∈D,\displaystyle z\in D, (6)
u⁡(z)=g⁡(z),\displaystyle u(z)=g(z), z∈∂D,\displaystyle z\in\partial D,

with Dirichlet boundary value g∈H12​(∂D)g\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\partial D) representing the voltage and the current source term is s=0s=0. The associated boundary observation operator Λa\Lambda_{a} is the well-known Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) map,

Λa:H1/2(∂D)↦H−1/2(∂D),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}:H^{1/2}(\partial D)\mapsto H^{-1/2}(\partial D), (7)
Λa[g]=a∂u∂ν|∂D,∀g∈H1/2(∂D),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}[g]=a\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}\Big|_{\partial D},~\forall g\in H^{1/2}(\partial D),

which maps the input voltage gg into the current a(z)∂u∂ν=a∇u⋅νa(z)\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=a\,\nabla u\cdot\nu (with ν\nu being the unit outward normal vector) at the boundary and uu is the solution of (6).

The inverse problem, often referred to as the Calderón problem, constitutes the basis of EIT Uhlmann (2009). It aims to find the conductivity aa of the medium, given different measurements of the DtN (voltage-to-current) pairs. Thus, this inverse problem falls into the considered abstract formalism and the inverse map (4) is given by,

ℱ−1:ℒ(H1/2(∂D),H−1/2(∂D))↦C2(D),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}:\mathcal{L}\left(H^{1/2}(\partial D),H^{-1/2}(\partial D)\right)\mapsto C^{2}(D), (8)
ℱ−1:Λa↦a=ℱ−1​(Λa),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}:\Lambda_{a}\mapsto a=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a}),

with ℒ⁡(⋅,⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot,\cdot) denoting the corresponding bounded linear operators. This inverse problem is shown to be well-defined and (logarithmic-) stable Clop et al. (2010).

2.3 Inverse Wave Scattering.

In many applications of interest, wave propagation in the frequency domain is used to infer material properties of the medium, modelled by the squared slowness 0<a∈L∞​(D)0<a\in L^{\infty}(D). The associated PDE is the Helmholtz equation,

−Δ​u−ω2​a​(z)​u=0,\displaystyle-\Delta u-\omega^{2}a(z)u=0, z∈D,\displaystyle z\in D, (9)
u⁡(z)=g⁡(z),\displaystyle u(z)=g(z), z∈∂D,\displaystyle z\in\partial D,

for some frequency ω\omega and Dirichlet boundary condition g∈H12​(∂D)g\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\partial D). The resulting boundary observation operator is again the Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) map

Λa:H1/2(∂D)↦H−1/2(∂D),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}:H^{1/2}(\partial D)\mapsto H^{-1/2}(\partial D), (10)
Λa[g]=∂u∂ν|∂D,∀g∈H1/2(∂D),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}[g]=\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}\Big|_{\partial D},~\forall g\in H^{1/2}(\partial D),

where uu is the solution to (9) with the coefficient aa. The corresponding inverse problem amounts to inferring the wave coefficient aa from the DtN map (10). Thus, it can be formulated similar to the inverse map (8). Its well-posedness and stability have been demonstrated for the Helmholtz equation in Nachman (1988) and references therein.

2.4 Radiative Transport and Optical Imaging.

In optical imaging or tomography, the material properties of the medium D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} are expressed in terms of the scattering and absorption coefficients, 0≤a,σa∈C⁡(D)0\leq a,\sigma_{a}\in C(D). The associated PDE is the well-known radiative transport equation (RTE) for the particle density u⁡(z,v)u(z,v) at location z∈Dz\in D and velocity v∈V⊂ℝdv\in V\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, given by

v⋅∇zu​(z,v)+σa​(z)​u​(z,v)=1ε​a​(z)​𝒬​[u],\displaystyle v\cdot\nabla_{z}u(z,v)+\sigma_{a}(z)u(z,v)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}a(z)\mathcal{Q}[u], z∈D,\displaystyle z\in D, (11)
u⁡(z,v)=ϕ⁡(z,v),\displaystyle u(z,v)=\phi(z,v), z∈Γ−,\displaystyle z\in\Gamma_{-},

where 𝒬⁡[u]=∫k⁡(v,v′)​u​(z,v′)​d​v′−u⁡(z,v)\mathcal{Q}[u]=\int k(v,v^{\prime})u(z,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}-u(z,v) is the collision term, ε\varepsilon is the Knudsen number, Γ±={(z,v)∈∂D×V:±nz⋅v≥0}\Gamma_{\pm}=\{(z,v)\in\partial D\times V:\pm\,n_{z}\cdot v\geq 0\} are the inflow (outflow) boundaries and nzn_{z} is the unit outer normal vector at z∈∂Dz\in\partial D. Thus, the input to this problem is provided by the particle density, uΓ−∈L1​(∂D)u_{\Gamma_{-}}\in L^{1}(\partial D), prescribed on the inflow boundary. The associated boundary observation operator Λa\Lambda_{a} defined in (2) is the so-called Albedo operator,

Λa:L1​(Γ−)↦L1​(Γ+),Λa:u|Γ−=ϕ↦u|Γ+,\Lambda_{a}:L^{1}(\Gamma_{-})\mapsto L^{1}(\Gamma_{+}),~\Lambda_{a}:u\big|_{\Gamma_{-}}=\phi\mapsto u\big|_{\Gamma_{+}}, (12)

that maps the incident boundary values on Γ−\Gamma_{-} to the observed boundary values on the outflow boundary Γ+\Gamma_{+}.

The corresponding inverse problem aims to infer the medium properties characterized by the scattering and absorption coefficients a,σaa,\sigma_{a} from the measurements of the Albedo operator. It leads to the following inverse map,

ℱ−1:ℒ⁡(L1​(Γ−),L1​(Γ+))↦C⁡(D),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}:\mathcal{L}\left(L^{1}(\Gamma_{-}),L^{1}(\Gamma_{+})\right)\mapsto C(D), (13)
ℱ−1:Λa↦a=ℱ−1​(Λa).\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}:\Lambda_{a}\mapsto a=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a}).

The well-posedness and Lipschitz-stability of this inverse map were shown in Bal & Jollivet (2008).

2.5 Seismic Imaging.

Seismic imaging is widely used in geophysics to infer and reconstruct sub-surface material properties for various applications such as CO2\text{CO}_{2} storage monitoring and seismic hazard assessment. Given a domain D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, we are interested in reconstructing the velocity coefficient 0<a∈L∞​(D)0<a\in L^{\infty}(D) by sending in acoustic waves from the top boundary into the medium and measuring the response in the time domain. The associated PDE is the acoustic wave equation,

ut​t(t,z)+a2(z)Δu=s,(z,t)∈D×[0,T],\displaystyle u_{tt}(t,z)+a^{2}(z)\Delta u=s,~(z,t)\in D\times[0,T], (14)

with a time-dependent source term ss. Here, uu is the pressure variation. The wave equation is supplemented with zero initial conditions, i.e., u⁡(⋅,0)=ut​(⋅,0)=0u(\cdot,0)=u_{t}(\cdot,0)=0 and suitable boundary conditions. In particular, sources are placed on a subset of the boundary and it is common to consider point sources s⁡(t,z)=g⁡(t)​δS​(z)s(t,z)=g(t)\delta_{S}(z) with g⁡(t)∈L2​([0,T])g(t)\in L^{2}([0,T]) and δS​(z)\delta_{S}(z) being the Dirac measure concentrated on a set S⊂∂DS\subset\partial D. These waves are transmitted, reflected, and refracted through the medium. Under certain assumptions (see Sec. 2.3 in Symes (2009)), the effective source ss can be treated as in L2​([0,T]×D)L^{2}([0,T]\times D), which ensures the well-posedness of the PDE. The resulting signal is recorded at a set of receivers ℛ⊂∂D\mathcal{R}\subset\partial D on the boundary that take continuous measurement in time [0,T][0,T]. The boundary observation operator (2) for this wave inverse problem is the Source-to-Receiver (StR) operator,

Λa:L2​([0,T]×D)↦L2​([0,T],Xℛ),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}:L^{2}([0,T]\times D)\mapsto L^{2}([0,T];X_{\mathcal{R}}), (15)
Λa:s↦u|[0,T]×ℛ,\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}:s\mapsto u\big|_{[0,T]\times\mathcal{R}},

where XℛX_{\mathcal{R}} is the metric space for the (discrete) set ℛ\mathcal{R}. The inverse problem that underpins seismic imaging is

ℱ−1:\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}: ℒ⁡(L2​([0,T]×D),L2​([0,T],Xℛ))↦L∞​(D),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\left(L^{2}([0,T]\times D),L^{2}([0,T];X_{\mathcal{R}})\right)\mapsto L^{\infty}(D), (16)
ℱ−1:\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}: Λa↦a=ℱ−1​(Λa),\displaystyle\Lambda_{a}\mapsto a=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a}),

with Λa\Lambda_{a} being the StR operator (15). Thus, seismic imaging aims to infer the subsurface spatial medium properties from spatial-temporal StR signals. This process is also termed as migration, or Full waveform Inversion (FWI) in the literature Deng et al. (2021). There have been studies on the well-posedness of the inverse problem for the wave equation (14) Liu & Oksanen (2016); Stefanov et al. (2016); Caday et al. (2019) although they do not directly apply to the setting considered here.

3 Neural Inverse Operators.

In this section, we present the neural network architecture for the proposed Neural Inverse Operators (NIOs).

3.1 Learning Task and Challenges.

All four examples described in the previous section were particular instances of the abstract framework summarized in (4). Thus, the solution of the inverse problem (4) boils down to inferring (learning) the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} from relevant data. Given sufficient training data in the form of pairs (Λa,ℱ−1​(Λa))\left(\Lambda_{a},\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a})\right) (or given the injectivity of the forward map, data in the form of pairs (a,Λa)\left(a,\Lambda_{a}\right)), we aim to learn the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} and evaluate it on test (unseen) data. This task is very challenging on account of the following factors:

  1. 1.

    The inputs to the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4) are specified on the boundaries ∂Ω\partial\Omega whereas the output is the coefficient aa, defined in the interior of the underlying domain DD. Thus, there is a mismatch in the domains of the inputs and outputs for the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1}.

  2. 2.

    The learning task requires us to learn mappings from operators to functions for ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} defined in (4).

  3. 3.

    In general, the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4) may only be weakly stable, for instance, either in terms of small values of the Hölder exponent α\alpha in (5) or even only logarithmic-stable. In these cases, the learning task can be very sensitive to noises from the input, and additional regularization terms might be necessary.

3.2 Existing Operator Learning Architectures.

Before proposing a suitable architectures for learning the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4), we briefly summarize existing operator learning architectures to examine whether they can be useful in this context. To this end, let D⊂ℝdx,U⊂ℝduD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}},U\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}} and 𝒳=𝒳⁡(D)\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}(D) and 𝒴=𝒴⁡(U)\mathcal{Y}=\mathcal{Y}(U) be suitable function spaces. Then, a DeepONet Lu et al. (2021) is the operator, 𝒩DON:𝒳→𝒴\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{DON}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}, given by

𝒩DON​(u¯)​(y)=∑k=1pβk​(u¯)​τk​(y),u¯∈𝒳,y∈U,\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{DON}}(\overline{u})(y)=\sum_{k=1}^{p}\beta_{k}(\overline{u})\tau_{k}(y),\quad\overline{u}\in\mathcal{X},\;y\in U, (17)

where the branch-net 𝜷\bm{\beta} is a neural network that maps ℰ⁡(u¯)=(u¯​(x1),…,u¯​(xm))∈ℝm\mathcal{E}(\overline{u})=(\overline{u}(x_{1}),\dots,\overline{u}(x_{m}))\in\mathbb{R}^{m}, evaluations of the input u¯\overline{u} at sensor points 𝒙:=(x1,…,xm)∈D\bm{x}:=(x_{1},\dots,x_{m})\in D, to ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}:

𝜷:ℝm→ℝp,ℰ⁡(u¯)↦(β1​(ℰ⁡(u¯)),…,βp​(ℰ⁡(u¯))CLOSE,\displaystyle\bm{\beta}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{p},~\mathcal{E}(\overline{u})\mapsto(\beta_{1}(\mathcal{E}(\overline{u})),\dots,\beta_{p}(\mathcal{E}(\overline{u})), (18)

and the trunk-net 𝝉⁡(y)=(τ1​(y),…,τp​(y))\bm{\tau}(y)=(\tau_{1}(y),\dots,\tau_{p}(y)) is another neural network mapping,

𝝉:U→ℝp,y↦(τ1​(y),…,τp​(y)).\displaystyle\bm{\tau}:U\to\mathbb{R}^{p},\quad y\mapsto(\tau_{1}(y),\dots,\tau_{p}(y)). (19)

Thus, a DeepONet combines the branch net (as coefficient functions) and trunk net (as basis functions) to create a mapping between functions.

On the other hand, a Fourier neural operator (FNO) 𝒩FNO\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{FNO}} (Li et al., 2021a) is a composition

𝒩FNO:𝒳↦𝒴:𝒩FNO=Q∘ℒT∘⋯∘ℒ1∘R.\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{FNO}}:\mathcal{X}\mapsto\mathcal{Y}:\quad\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{FNO}}=Q\circ\mathcal{L}_{T}\circ\dots\circ\mathcal{L}_{1}\circ R. (20)

For simplicity let us define ℳ=Q∘ℒT∘⋯∘ℒ1\mathcal{M}=Q\circ\mathcal{L}_{T}\circ\dots\circ\mathcal{L}_{1}, and 𝒩FNO=ℳ∘R\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{FNO}}=\mathcal{M}\circ R, where R:(x,u¯)↦R⁡(u¯​(x),x)R:(x,\overline{u})\mapsto R(\overline{u}(x),x) is a “lifting operator” represented by a linear transformation R:ℝdu×d→ℝdvR:\mathbb{R}^{{d_{u}}\times d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} where du{d_{u}} is the number of components of the input function, dd is the dimension of the domain and dvd_{v} is the “lifting dimension” (a hyperparameter). The operator QQ is a nonlinear projection, instantiated by a shallow neural network, such that vT+1​(x)↦𝒩FNO​(u¯)​(x)=Q⁡(vT+1​(x))v^{T+1}(x)\mapsto\mathcal{N}^{\mathrm{FNO}}(\overline{u})(x)=Q\left(v^{T+1}(x)\right). Each hidden layer ℒℓ:vℓ​(x)↦vℓ+1​(x)\mathcal{L}_{\ell}:v^{\ell}(x)\mapsto v^{\ell+1}(x) is of the form

vℓ+1​(x)=σ⁡(Wℓ⋅vℓ​(x)+bℓ​(x)+(Kℓ​vℓ)​(x)),v^{\ell+1}(x)=\sigma\left(W_{\ell}\cdot v^{\ell}(x)+b_{\ell}(x)+\left(K_{\ell}v^{\ell}\right)(x)\right),

with Wℓ∈ℝdv×dvW_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}\times d_{v}} a weight matrix (residual connection), bℓ​(x)∈ℝdvb_{\ell}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} a bias function, σ\sigma an activation function, and the non-local Fourier layer,

Kℓ​vℓ=ℱN−1​(Pℓ​(k)⋅ℱN​vℓ​(k)),K_{\ell}v^{\ell}=\mathcal{F}_{N}^{-1}\left(P_{\ell}(k)\cdot\mathcal{F}_{N}v^{\ell}(k)\right),

where ℱN​vℓ​(k)\mathcal{F}_{N}v^{\ell}(k) denotes the (truncated)-Fourier coefficients of the discrete Fourier transform (DFT) of vℓ​(x)v^{\ell}(x), computed based on the given NN grid values in each direction. Here, Pℓ​(k)∈ℂdv×dvP_{\ell}(k)\in\mathbb{C}^{d_{v}\times d_{v}} is a complex Fourier multiplication matrix indexed by k∈ℤdk\in\mathbb{Z}^{d}, and ℱN−1\mathcal{F}_{N}^{-1} denotes the inverse DFT.

Both operator learning frameworks (DeepONet and FNO) and their variants map functions to functions. Hence, they cannot directly be used to learn the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4), which maps operators to functions. Therefore, we need to modify and adapt these architectures to learn the inverse map. The following sections present our proposed approach.

3.3 A Motivating (Formal) Calculation.

We start by providing a heuristic motivation for our proposed architecture to learn the inverse map (4). To this end and for definiteness, we consider the inverse wave scattering problem for the Helmholtz equation (9), presented in section 2.3. Given the domain D⊂ℝdD\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, we consider the following eigenvalue problem with Neumann boundary conditions,

−Δ​φk\displaystyle-\Delta\varphi_{k} =λkφk,∀z∈D.\displaystyle=\lambda_{k}\varphi_{k},\quad\forall z\in D. (21)
∂φk∂ν|∂D\displaystyle\frac{\partial\varphi_{k}}{\partial\nu}\big|_{\partial D} =0,∫Dφkdz=0.\displaystyle=0,\quad\int\limits_{D}\varphi_{k}dz=0.

By standard PDE theory Evans (2010), there exist eigenvalues 0≤λk∈ℝ0\leq\lambda_{k}\in\mathbb{R} for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, and the corresponding eigenfunctions {φk}\{\varphi_{k}\} form an orthonormal basis for L2​(D)L^{2}(D). We fix K∈ℕK\in\mathbb{N} sufficiently large and without loss of generality, we assume ω=1\omega=1 in the Helmholtz equation (9) to consider the following Dirichlet boundary value problems,

−Δ​uk−a⁡(z)​uk=0,\displaystyle-\Delta u_{k}-a(z)u_{k}=0, z∈D,1≤k≤K,\displaystyle z\in D,~1\leq k\leq K, (22)
u​(z)=gk​(z),\displaystyle u(z)=g_{k}(z), z∈∂D,\displaystyle z\in\partial D,

where gk=φk|∂Dg_{k}=\varphi_{k}\big|_{\partial D}. Using (21) and (22), we prove in SM B, the following formal representation formula for all 1≤k≤K1\leq k\leq K,

∫Da​uk​φk​𝑑z=∫Dλk​uk​φk​𝑑z−∫∂Dgk​∂uk∂ν​𝑑σ​(z).\int\limits_{D}au_{k}\varphi_{k}dz=\int\limits_{D}\lambda_{k}u_{k}\varphi_{k}dz-\int\limits_{\partial D}g_{k}\frac{\partial u_{k}}{\partial\nu}d\sigma(z). (23)

The formula (23) can be used to construct an approximation to the coefficient a∈L2​(D)a\in L^{2}(D) in the following manner. Writing a≈∑ℓ=1Kaℓ​φℓa\approx\sum\limits_{\ell=1}^{K}a_{\ell}\varphi_{\ell} (using the orthonormality of φ\varphi’s) for KK sufficiently large, we can evaluate the coefficients aℓa_{\ell} by solving the following Matrix equation for A={aℓ}ℓ=1KA=\{a_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{K},

𝐂​A\displaystyle{\bf C}A =B,𝐂k​ℓ=∫Dukφkφldx,∀k,l,\displaystyle=B,~{\bf C}_{k\ell}=\int\limits_{D}u_{k}\varphi_{k}\varphi_{l}dx,\quad\forall k,l, (24)
Bk\displaystyle B_{k} =∫Dλk​uk​φk​dz+∫∂Dgk​∂uk∂ν​dσ​(z),∀k.\displaystyle=\int\limits_{D}\lambda_{k}u_{k}\varphi_{k}dz+\int\limits_{\partial D}g_{k}\frac{\partial u_{k}}{\partial\nu}d\sigma(z),\forall k.

Further setting Ψk=∂uk∂ν\Psi_{k}=\frac{\partial u_{k}}{\partial\nu}, we observe that the formal approximation of the coefficient aa relies on the following building blocks,

  • •

    Basis Construction: The operations ℬk:z↦(φk​(z),λk)\mathcal{B}_{k}:z\mapsto\left(\varphi_{k}(z),\lambda_{k}\right), 1≤k≤K1\leq k\leq K, that form a basis. Note that they are independent of the coefficient aa.

  • •

    PDE Solve: The operation ℰk:(gk,Ψk)↦({ujk}j=1K,∫∂Dgk​Ψk​𝑑σ​(z))\mathcal{E}_{k}:(g_{k},\Psi_{k})\mapsto\big(\{u^{k}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{K},\int\limits_{\partial D}g_{k}\Psi_{k}d\sigma(z)\big) that amounts to (approximately) inferring the coefficients of the solution uku_{k} of the Helmholtz equation (22), given the Dirichlet gkg_{k} and Neumann Ψk\Psi_{k} boundary values. A part of the right-hand side term BkB_{k} is also appended to this operation. Once the coefficients ujku^{k}_{j} are computed, the approximation uku_{k} to the solution of (22) is readily computed in terms of the basis {φk}\{\varphi_{k}\} by setting uk≈∑j=1Kujk​φju_{k}\approx\sum\limits_{j=1}^{K}u^{k}_{j}\varphi_{j}.

  • •

    Mode Mixing: The previous two operations were restricted to individual modes, i.e., to each kk, for 1≤k≤K1\leq k\leq K. However, to construct the coefficients 𝐂k​l{\bf C}_{kl} in (24), we need to mix different modes. One way to do so is through multiplication. We denote this operation by ℳ:({φk}k=1K,{uk}k=1K)↦({uk​φk​φℓ}k,ℓ=1K,{λk​uk​φk}k=1K)\mathcal{M}:\left(\{\varphi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K},\{u_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)\mapsto\left(\{u_{k}\varphi_{k}\varphi_{\ell}\}_{k,\ell=1}^{K},\{\lambda_{k}u_{k}\varphi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right).

  • •

    Matrix Inversion: In the final step, we need to build the Matrix 𝐂{\bf C} in (24) and (approximately) invert it. This operation can be summarized by ℐ:({uk​φk​φℓ}k,ℓ=1K,{λk​uk​φk}k=1K)↦∑j=1Kaj​φj\mathcal{I}:\left(\{u_{k}\varphi_{k}\varphi_{\ell}\}_{k,\ell=1}^{K},\{\lambda_{k}u_{k}\varphi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\right)\mapsto\sum_{j=1}^{K}a_{j}\varphi_{j}, with A={aj}A=\{a_{j}\} being the solution of (24).

3.4 The Architecture.

The formal approximation of the inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4) for the Helmholtz equation by formulas (23)-(24) cannot be directly used in practice as one cannot solve the PDE (22) without knowing the coefficient aa. However, the building blocks enumerated above motivate either an iterative fixed-point procedure or, in our case, a learning algorithm approximating ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} from data. To this end, we observe that the basis construction z↦φk​(z)z\mapsto\varphi_{k}(z) amounts to a particular instantiation of a trunk-net (19) of a DeepONet. Similarly, the PDE solve map ℰk:(gk,Ψk)↦{ujk}j=1K\mathcal{E}_{k}:(g_{k},\Psi_{k})\mapsto\{u^{k}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{K} is a particular instance of the application of a branch-net (18) of a DeepONet. Moreover, they can be combined in a DeepONet (17) to approximate the solutions uku_{k} of the PDE (22). However, a DeepONet (17) is linear in its trunk-net basis functions and thus cannot represent the nonlinear mode mixing operator ℳ\mathcal{M}. Instead, one can do so by passing the outputs of the DeepONet to the nonlinear layers of an FNO (20), which also performs the final inversion operator ℐ\mathcal{I}.

These heuristic considerations are generalized to the abstract formalism of the inverse problem (4) and motivate us to propose the composition (stacking) of DeepONets and FNO to result in the following map,

𝒩N​I​O:(z{Ψℓ}ℓ=1L)​⟼τ,β​({τk​(z)}k=1p{βk}k=1p)​…\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{NIO}:\begin{pmatrix}z\\ \{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\end{pmatrix}\overset{\tau,\beta}{\longmapsto}\begin{pmatrix}\{\tau_{k}(z)\}_{k=1}^{p}\\ \{\beta_{k}\}_{k=1}^{p}\end{pmatrix}\ldots (25)
…​⟼𝒩D​O​N​{fℓ​(z)}ℓ=1L​⟼𝑅​h​(z)​⟼ℳ​a∗​(z),\displaystyle\ldots\overset{\mathcal{N}^{DON}}{\longmapsto}\{f_{\ell}(z)\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\overset{R}{\longmapsto}h(z)\overset{\mathcal{M}}{\longmapsto}a^{\ast}(z),

for approximating the abstract inverse map ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} (4). Here, the linear map RR can be explicitly defined as

h⁡(z)=R⁡(f1,…,fL,z)=\displaystyle h(z)=R(f_{1},\dots,f_{L},z)= 1L​∑ℓ=1LDℓ​fℓ+E​z,\displaystyle\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}D_{\ell}f_{\ell}+Ez, (26)

with E,Dℓ∈ℝdvE,D_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}}. In other words, the inputs z∈Dz\in D and Ψℓ=Λa​(gℓ)\Psi_{\ell}=\Lambda_{a}(g_{\ell}) (2), for 1≤ℓ≤L1\leq\ell\leq L, are fed into the trunk- and branch-nets of a DeepONet 𝒩D​O​N\mathcal{N}^{DON} (17), respectively, to create LL representations {fℓ}ℓ=1L\{f_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}, defined in the interior of the underlying domain. These representations are first linearly transformed through RR yielding h⁡(z)h(z), and finally mixed by the nonlinear component ℳ\mathcal{M} of FNO resulting in an approximation of the underlying coefficient a∗a^{\ast}. We observe that the DeepONet 𝒩D​O​N\mathcal{N}^{DON} in 𝒩N​I​O\mathcal{N}^{NIO} (25) is flexible enough to handle inputs defined on the boundary, i.e., Ψℓ\Psi_{\ell}, and produce outputs fℓf_{\ell}, defined on the interior of the underlying domain.

It is important to note that the model takes only zz and {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} as input, rather than zz and the input-output pair {(gℓ,Ψℓ)}ℓ=1L\{(g_{\ell},\Psi_{\ell})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. This choice is motivated by the following consideration: let us define μg\mu_{g} as the underlying measure (distribution) on the boundary data gg, where gℓ∼μgg_{\ell}\sim\mu_{g}, and μΨ=Λa​#​μg\mu_{\Psi}=\Lambda_{a}\#\mu_{g} represents the pushforward measure given the boundary operator Λa\Lambda_{a}. Hence, Ψℓ∼μΨ\Psi_{\ell}\sim\mu_{\Psi} for all ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,...,L, with {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} representing the empirical distribution approximating μΨ\mu_{\Psi}. This, together with the injectivity of the boundary observation operator (2), implies that {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} suffices to provide statistical information about the operator Λa\Lambda_{a} given μg\mu_{g} satisfying certain properties. We denote LL as the number of samples discretizing the measure μΨ\mu_{\Psi} or, with abuse of notation, the operator Λa\Lambda_{a}.

The construction above addresses point (1) in Section 3.1. However, it does not necessarily satisfy point (2) in its current form. For the model to effectively process μΨ\mu_{\Psi} as the input rather than a particular discrete realization of it, the following desirable properties should be met:

  • •

    The architecture should exhibit invariance under permutations of the input measurements {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} as they are i.i.d. samples of μΨ\mu_{\Psi}.

  • •

    The learning framework must be able to handle an empirical measure of the distribution μΨ\mu_{\Psi} with an arbitrary sample size L~\tilde{L}. In particular, the input sample size at the training and testing stages could be different.

  • •

    The performance of the model should be independent of the sample size L~\tilde{L} used to discretize μΨ\mu_{\Psi}.

To address the first two points, we can modify the architecture by redefining the linear transformation RR as follows:

h⁡(z)=R⁡(f1,…,fL,z)=DL​∑ℓ=1Lfℓ+E​z,E,D∈ℝdvh(z)=R(f_{1},\dots,f_{L},z)=\frac{D}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}f_{\ell}+Ez,\quad E,D\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{v}} (27)

To ensure the performance is independent of L~\tilde{L}, a naive and inefficient approach would involve constructing all possible permutations of {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} with size L^\widehat{L} for all L^=2,…,L\widehat{L}=2,\ldots,L and providing them as input to the model. However, inspired by the well-known bagging algorithm widely used in machine learning, we propose an efficient and novel method to tackle this point which we term randomized batching. In this approach, given the sequence {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}, during each training iteration, an integer number L^\widehat{L} is randomly drawn from the set {2,…,L}\{2,\ldots,L\}. Then, L^\widehat{L} samples are randomly picked from {Ψℓ}ℓ=1L\{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} and the new sequence {Ψk}k=1L^\{\Psi_{k}\}_{k=1}^{\widehat{L}} are fed into the model at each iteration during training.

We refer to the architecture (25) with the linear transformation RR given in (27), and incorporating the randomized batching algorithm, as Neural Inverse Operator (see Figure 1 for a schematic representation of the architecture).

4 Empirical Results.

We empirically test NIO on benchmark PDE inverse problems below. The exact details of the training, as well as the architecture and hyperparameter choices, are presented in SM D.

As baselines in the following experiments, we choose two models. First, we consider a DeepONet with a CNN as the branch net in (17), which performs mixing of the input function within the branch itself

𝒩D​O​N​e​t:(z{Ψℓ}ℓ=1L)​⟼τ,βc​o​n​({τk​(z)}k=1p{βk}k=1p)​⟼𝒩D​O​N​a∗​(z).\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{DONet}:\begin{pmatrix}z\\ \{\Psi_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\end{pmatrix}\overset{\tau,\beta_{con}}{\longmapsto}\begin{pmatrix}\{\tau_{k}(z)\}_{k=1}^{p}\\ \{\beta_{k}\}_{k=1}^{p}\end{pmatrix}\overset{\mathcal{N}^{DON}}{\longmapsto}a^{\ast}(z). (28)

Second, we consider a fully convolutional image-to-image neural network architecture (details in SM D.1). A variant of this architecture was already used in seismic imaging (full waveform inversion) in Deng et al. (2021). We have extended this architecture significantly to apply it to the abstract inverse problem (4).

4.1 Calderón Problem for EIT.

We start with the Calderón problem for the elliptic equation (6) on the computational domain D=[0,1]2D=[0,1]^{2}, with source s=0s=0. The training (and test) data are generated by sampling from a probability distribution on the conductivity coefficient aa. Once a sample conductivity is drawn, a set of Dirichlet boundary conditions {gℓ}ℓ=1L\{g_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} are drawn from a probability distribution on the boundary values. For each gℓg_{\ell}, the underlying elliptic equation is solved numerically with a standard five-point finite difference scheme and the current, Ψℓ=a​∂u∂ν\Psi_{\ell}=a\frac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}, is evaluated on the boundary. We choose the boundary data gℓg_{\ell}, for 1≤ℓ≤L=201\leq\ell\leq L=20 as the boundary values of cos⁡(ω⁡(x​cos⁡(θℓ)+y​sin⁡(θℓ)))\cos(\omega(x\cos(\theta_{\ell})+y\sin(\theta_{\ell}))), with θℓ=2​π​ℓ20\theta_{\ell}=\frac{2\pi\ell}{20}. For the coefficient aa, we sample from trigonometric functions by setting a⁡(x,y)=exp⁡(∑k=1mck​sin⁡(k​π​x)​sin⁡(k​π​y)),a(x,y)=\exp\big(\sum_{k=1}^{m}c_{k}\sin(k\pi x)\sin(k\pi y)\big), with m=mod(m¯)m=\mod(\overline{m}) where m¯∼𝒰⁡([1,5])\overline{m}\sim\mathcal{U}([1,5]) and {ck}∼𝒰⁡([−1,1]m)\{c_{k}\}\sim\mathcal{U}([-1,1]^{m}). All the models are trained with 40964096 training coefficient samples, and the relative (percentage) test errors (with respect to 20482048 test samples) in both L1L^{1} and L2L^{2} norms for NIO (and the baselines) are presented in Table 1. As the table shows, NIO is the best-performing model, outperforming the next-best FCNN model by almost halving the errors. Moreover, the total errors are very small (<1%<1\%) with NIO.

As a second experiment for EIT, we consider a more practical example suggested in Muller & Siltanen (2012), where the authors model the EIT imaging of the heart and lungs of a patient using electrodes on the body. This discontinuous heart and lungs phantom is depicted in SM Figure 6. The underlying domain is the unit circle, and the elliptic equation (6) is solved with a standard finite element scheme. The boundary conditions are given by gℓ​(θ)=12​π​exp⁡(i​2​π​θ​fℓ)g_{\ell}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\exp(i2\pi\theta f_{\ell}), with ℓ=1,…,32\ell=1,\ldots,32 and f=[−16,…,−1,1,14,15,16]f=[-16,\ldots,-1,1,14,15,16]. The coefficient aa is modelled by adding 8%8\% white noise to the location, shape, and conductivity of the configuration of heart and lungs shown in SM Figure 6. The input of the learning operators is obtained by computing the Fourier transform at frequencies ff of the difference between the Neumann trace of the PDE solution with the coefficient aa and the one with the unit coefficient a=1a=1. Again, the results presented in Table 1 and 2 show that NIO is the best-performing model and yields very low reconstruction errors, solving this practical problem with high accuracy. In contrast, a traditional direct method such as the D-bar method Muller & Siltanen (2012) has a larger error of 8.75%8.75\% for this numerical inversion test (see SM Section E.8 for details).

4.2 Inverse Wave Scattering.

In this problem, the Helmholtz equation (9) is considered on the domain D=[0,1]2D=[0,1]^{2}, and the task is to learn coefficients sampled from a distribution, a⁡(x,y)=∑k=1mexp⁡(−c​(x−c1,k)4−c​(y−c2,k)4),a(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\exp\big(-c(x-c_{1,k})^{4}-c(y-c_{2,k})^{4}\big), with c=2×104/3c=2\times 10^{4}/3. It represents a homogeneous medium with square-shaped inclusions, randomly spread in the domain (see SM Figure 8). Here, m=mod(m¯)m=\mod(\overline{m}), m¯∼𝒰⁡([1,4])\overline{m}\sim\mathcal{U}([1,4]) and {(c1,k,c2,k)}∼𝒰⁡([0,1]m×2)\{(c_{1,k},c_{2,k})\}\sim\mathcal{U}([0,1]^{m\times 2}). For each draw of the coefficient, 2020 Dirichlet boundary values are prescribed, exactly as in the EIT experiment with trigonometric coefficients. The corresponding (approximate) solutions of the Helmholtz equation (9) are computed with a central finite difference scheme, and the Neumann trace is evaluated to represent the DtN map. We train the models with 40964096 training samples and present the relative (median) test errors, on a test set of 16001600 samples, in Table 1. Again, NIO is the best-performing model, beating the next-best FCNN by a significant margin.

4.3 Radiative Transport Equation and Optical Imaging.

Next, we consider the radiative transport equation (11) in the domain X×VX\times V, where X=[0,1]X=[0,1] and V=[−1,1]V=[-1,1], with ε=1\varepsilon=1. Consequently, Γ−={(0,v),v∈[0,1]}∪{(1,v),v∈[−1,0]}\Gamma_{-}=\{(0,v),v\in[0,1]\}\cup\{(1,v),v\in[-1,0]\}. The task is to infer the absorption and scattering coefficients from the Albedo operator (12). To this end, we fix k⁡(v,v′)=1k(v,v^{\prime})=1, σa=1−a\sigma_{a}=1-a in (11) and draw the absorption coefficient aa from the distribution, a(x)=cχ[−1/2,1/2](rx−x0)+1a(x)=c\chi_{[-1/2,1/2]}(rx-x_{0})+1, with χ\chi denoting the characteristic function and with c∼𝒰⁡([0.5,1])c\sim\mathcal{U}([0.5,1]), x0∼𝒰⁡([0,1])x_{0}\sim\mathcal{U}([0,1]) and r∼𝒰⁡([0,0.8])r\sim\mathcal{U}([0,0.8]). Once the coefficient is drawn, boundary conditions on the inflow boundary Γ−\Gamma_{-} are imposed by setting ϕℓ​(0,v)=exp⁡(−200​(v−vℓ)2)\phi_{\ell}(0,v)=\exp{\big(-200\left(v-v_{\ell}\right)^{2}\big)}, and ϕℓ​(1,v)=0\phi_{\ell}(1,v)=0, if vℓ>0v_{\ell}>0, and ϕℓ​(0,v)=0\phi_{\ell}(0,v)=0, and ϕℓ​(1,v)=exp⁡(−200​(v−vℓ)2)\phi_{\ell}(1,v)=\exp{\big(-200\left(v-v_{\ell}\right)^{2}\big)}, if vℓ<0v_{\ell}<0, with vℓv_{\ell} being the ℓ\ell-th quadrature point used to approximate the integral term in (11), 1≤ℓ≤321\leq\ell\leq 32. Then, the radiative transport equation is approximated with a finite-element method, and the resulting solution uℓu_{\ell} is evaluated at the outflow boundary Γ+\Gamma_{+} as the output of the Albedo operator (12). All the models are trained on 40964096 training samples, and the relative median test errors on a test set of 20482048 samples are presented in Table 1, demonstrating that NIO significantly outperforms both FCNN and DeepONet, also in this case, resulting in low test errors even for the underlying discontinuous absorption coefficient.

4.4 Seismic Imaging.

In the final test, we model seismic imaging by considering the acoustic wave equation (14) in the space-time domain [0,1]2×[0,T][0,1]^{2}\times[0,T] and the task at hand is to learn the underlying squared-slowness coefficients aa from the source-to-receiver map (15). To this end, we choose two types of coefficients from Deng et al. (2021), the so-called Style-A and CurveVel-A datasets. For each medium, waves are generated at source locations (xsℓ,0)(x_{s_{\ell},0}) on the vertical boundary, for ℓ=1,…,5\ell=1,\ldots,5. The corresponding acoustic wave equation is solved with a finite difference scheme, and the temporal data is recorded at receivers on the vertical boundary. We follow Deng et al. (2021) and train all the models with 5500055000 and 2200022000 training samples for the Style-A and CurveVel-A datasets, respectively, and present the resulting (median) relative test errors, on a test set of 70007000 and 60006000 samples, in Table 1. We observe from the table that even for this problem, NIO is either outperforming or on par with FCNN. This is particularly noteworthy as the FCNN architecture was demonstrated to be one of the states of the art on this problem in Deng et al. (2021) among several machine learning models.

4.5 Robustness and Computational Efficiency of NIO.

In the SM E, we provide further details on the performance of NIO and its comparison to the considered baselines in terms of several factors. Here, we present a succinct summary of these results. First, inverse problems are characterized by sensitivity to perturbations of different types. Hence, it is imperative to test the robustness of the proposed NIO framework to these factors. To this end, we start with adding noise to the inputs of each of the benchmarks at test time and present the resulting test errors in SM Table 8 to observe that NIO (as well as the baselines) are not sensitive to this noise. Next, in SM Table 9, we plot the test errors for the models when the underlying grid resolution is varied at test time to observe that NIO is not sensitive to the input grid resolution. Finally, in SM Table 10, we present errors when the locations of input sensors are chosen randomly at test time, in contrast to sensors located on a uniform grid at training, to see that NIO is also robust to this variation. However, these factors are less salient in this context than the discretization of the input boundary observation operator. The key element of this discretization is the number of input samples. As argued in the previous section, NIO has been constructed to be independent of the number of samples that discretize the boundary observation operator. We test this behavior for the inverse wave scattering problem (see SM E.2 for other benchmarks) and present the errors in Figure 2, where the number of input samples at the testing stage are decreased (left) and increased (right) at test time. We clearly see that NIO is very robust to this fluctuation, completely contrasting to the baselines whose performance deteriorates, and the test errors increase by almost an order of magnitude. This demonstrates that NIO genuinely learns the underlying inverse map rather than just a discrete representation of it. Finally, in SM E.6, it is shown that NIO generalizes very well out-of-distribution for a variety of problems, outperforming baselines considerably.

We conclude this section by comparing NIO with the well-established PDE-constrained optimization algorithms. To this end, we consider an out-of-distribution example for the inverse wave scattering benchmark and compare the results of NIO and PDE-constrained optimization (see details in SM E.8) in Figure 2 (Right) to observe that NIO is much more accurate in reconstructing the scatterers than PDE-constrained optimization. The L1L^{1}-test errors are 2.3%2.3\% for NIO and 11.1%11.1\% for PDE-constrained optimization. Moreover, it took less than 11 sec of inference time for NIO (on a CPU) compared to a single GPU training time of 8.58.5 hours for the PDE-constrained optimization problem. Thus, this experiment demonstrates the real efficiency of NIO as it is 55 times more accurate while being 44 orders of magnitude faster than the PDE-constrained optimization algorithm.

5 Related Work.

Existing methods for solving the class of PDE inverse problems considered here include the so-called Direct Methods, such as the D-bar method Isaacson et al. (2004) for EIT and the so-called Imaging condition Claerbout (1985) for seismic inversion. Iterative methods approximating fixed points Bakushinsky & Kokurin (2005) are also used, including the very popular gradient-based PDE-constrained optimization methods Chavent (2010). Another approach falls in the category of Bayesian formulation of inverse problems Tarantola (2005); Stuart (2010), which also quantifies the uncertainty of the solution. Finally, directly learning some PDE inverse operators from data has been considered in Maarten et al. (2022) and references therein.

6 Discussion.

For PDEs, written in the abstract form (1), we consider a large class of inverse problems that are only well-defined when the underlying inverse operator (4), maps an operator (the boundary observation operator (2)) to the underlying coefficient (a function). The resulting inverse problem amounts to inferring the unknown coefficient aa from data pairs (Λa,ℱ−1​(Λa))(\Lambda_{a},\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\Lambda_{a})) representing the observation operator. Existing operator learning frameworks such as DeepONets (17) and FNOs (20) only map functions to functions. Hence, one needs to adapt them to be able to learn mappings between operators and functions in order to solve the inverse problem (4). To this end, we have proposed a novel architecture, termed Neural Inverse Operators (NIO), based on a composition of DeepONets and FNOs, augmented with suitable architectural priors (definition of RR in (27)), and trained with randomized batching, to guarantee invariance of the generalization error to the different discretization of the input operator. Our architecture is motivated by the underlying structure of the inverse map. We tested the NIO on a variety of benchmark inverse problems. These include the Calderón Problem in electrical impedance tomography, inverse wave scattering modelled with the Helmholtz equation, optical imaging using the radiative transport equation, and seismic imaging with the acoustic wave equation. For all these problems, NIO outperformed baselines significantly and provided accurate and, more importantly, robust approximations to the unknown coefficients with small errors (see SM E). Finally, a series of experiments were also presented to demonstrate that NIO is robust with respect to various factors such as varying sensor locations, grid resolutions, noise, and discretizations of the input operator while being able to generalize out-of-distribution and being more accurate and much faster than direct and PDE constrained optimization algorithms. As this is the first paper where an end-to-end machine learning framework is proposed for learning maps between operators and functions, various extensions are possible. For instance, other architectures, such as recently proposed LOCA Kissas et al. (2022), VIDON Prasthofer et al. (2022), or graph-based approaches Boussif et al. (2022); Brandstetter et al. (2022), can be adapted in this context. Problems in higher-dimensional (particularly with seismic) imaging need to be considered to explore how NIOs scale with increasing problem size. Finally, approximation bounds and universality results, in the spirit of Lanthaler et al. (2022); Kovachki et al. (2021a) need to be derived in order to place NIOs on a solid theoretical footing.

Appendix B Proof of Formula (23) in Main Text.

Below, we prove the representation formula (23) in the main text.

Proof.

Multiplying uku_{k} (the solution of (22)) to Eqn (21) and integrating over space, we obtain,

∫Duk​Δ​φk​𝑑z+λk​∫Dφk​𝑑z=0\int\limits_{D}u_{k}\Delta\varphi_{k}dz+\lambda_{k}\int\limits_{D}\varphi_{k}dz=0

Integrating by parts in the above equation and using the Gauss-Green formula yields,

−∫D⟨∇uk,∇φk⟩dz+∫∂Duk∂φk∂ν⏟=0ds(z)+λk∫Dukφkdz=0.-\int\limits_{D}\langle\nabla u_{k},\nabla\varphi_{k}\rangle dz+\int\limits_{\partial D}u_{k}\underbrace{\frac{\partial\varphi_{k}}{\partial\nu}}_{=0}ds(z)+\lambda_{k}\int\limits_{D}u_{k}\varphi_{k}dz=0. (29)

Note that the Neumann boundary conditions from (21) in the above.

Similarly, multiplying the solution φk\varphi_{k} of the Neumann problem (21) to the Eqn (22) and repeating the above integration parts yields,

−∫D⟨∇uk,∇φk⟩dz+∫∂Dgk∂uk∂νds(z)+∫Da(z)ukφkdz=0.-\int\limits_{D}\langle\nabla u_{k},\nabla\varphi_{k}\rangle dz+\int\limits_{\partial D}g_{k}\frac{\partial u_{k}}{\partial\nu}ds(z)+\int\limits_{D}a(z)u_{k}\varphi_{k}dz=0. (30)

Appendix D Architecture and Training Details

Below, details concerning the model architectures and training are discussed. The implementation of the experiments of the paper is realized within the PyTorch framework and available at
